classification.difficultyReason: Recognise the two-day interval and combined approach rate to find initial separation, then distinguish the rocket travel distance from that separation; taught closing-speed model.

content.prompt: A meteor is heading straight for Earth at a speed of 90 000 km/h. A rocket is launched towards the meteor at a speed through space of 20 000 km/h. If it takes the rocket two days to collide with and destroy the meteor, how far from Earth is it when the rocket is launched, and how far from Earth does the collision take place?

answer.short: Initially $5\,280\,000\text{ km}$ from Earth; collision $960\,000\text{ km}$ from Earth.
answer.worked: Two days is $48\text{ h}$. As the meteor and rocket approach one another, their closing speed is $90\,000+20\,000=110\,000\text{ km/h}$. Hence their initial separation is $110\,000\times48=5\,280\,000\text{ km}$. The rocket travels $20\,000\times48=960\,000\text{ km}$ from Earth before collision. Check: the meteor travels $90\,000\times48=4\,320\,000\text{ km}$, and the two distances sum to $5\,280\,000\text{ km}$.
